title: Mapping-space detection of levelwise equivalences between complete Segal spaces
statement:
Use small simplicial sets, Kan complexes, homotopy fibers and weak homotopy equivalences from [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones], the Kan model structure from [lem-coef-kan-quillen-right-proper], and Reedy fibrancy and functorial Reedy replacement from [lem-coef-reedy-model-structure]. A simplicial space is a functor $W:\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathrm{sSet}$, equivalently represented by the strictly curried bisimplicial set used below. In this statement a Segal space is Reedy fibrant and its consecutive-edge maps $W_n\to W_1\times_{W_0}\cdots\times_{W_0}W_1$ are weak homotopy equivalences for every $n\geq2$. Write $M_W(x,y)$ for the strict fiber of $(d_1,d_0):W_1\to W_0\times W_0$ at vertices $(x,y)$; Reedy fibrancy makes this a Kan complex representing the homotopy fiber. Its homotopy category $hW$ has the vertices of $W_0$ as objects, morphisms $\pi_0M_W(x,y)$, identities induced by $s_0$, and composition induced by the degree-two Segal map and $d_1$. Let $W_{\mathrm{eq}}\subseteq W_1$ be the union of components representing isomorphisms in $hW$. Call $W$ complete if $s_0:W_0\to W_{\mathrm{eq}}$ is a weak homotopy equivalence.

Let $f:U\to V$ be a map between complete Segal spaces. Then $f_n:U_n\to V_n$ is a weak homotopy equivalence for every $n\geq0$ if and only if both of the following hold: for every pair of vertices $x,y\in U_0$, the induced map $M_U(x,y)\to M_V(fx,fy)$ is a weak homotopy equivalence; and every object of $hV$ is isomorphic to an object $f(x)$. No discreteness, connectedness or nonemptiness condition on $U_0,V_0$ is imposed.

source.place: Rezk, A model for the homotopy theory of homotopy theory, Proposition 7.6, printed pp. 16-17, with Section 7.4 and Proposition 6.4 for the meaning of Dwyer--Kan equivalence. Read online; not archived in literature/. No Stacks tag states this simplicial-homotopy result.

proof.text: For each $W=U,V$, apply [lem-coef-reedy-model-structure] with $\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}$ and the Kan model category. All $W_n$ are Kan, and the degree-one matching object is $W_0^2$, so $p_W=(d_1,d_0):W_1\to W_0^2$ is a Kan fibration. Products of Kan complexes are Kan, by solving a horn-lifting problem coordinatewise. Apply [lem-coef-kan-pullback-path-comparison] with $p_W$ and the vertex $(x,y)$ to identify the strict mapping fiber with its specified path-model homotopy fiber, naturally in $W$. The unital associative homotopy category and the induced functor $hf$ are supplied by [lem-coef-segal-homotopy-category-components].

source.place: Sections 4.1, 5.1-5.5; matching-fibration and strict/path-model comparison

proof.text: The component-invariance assertion of [lem-coef-segal-homotopy-category-components] identifies the strict fiber of $p_W^{\mathrm{eq}}:W_{\mathrm{eq}}\to W_0^2$ with the subspace $E_W(x,y)\subseteq M_W(x,y)$ consisting exactly of the isomorphism components. This restricted endpoint map is still a Kan fibration: solve a horn lifting problem using $p_W$; a horn in positive dimension contains a vertex, and every vertex of the resulting simplex is connected to that vertex, so the entire simplex remains in the selected union of components. Thus $W_{\mathrm{eq}}$ and all $E_W(x,y)$ are Kan. The strict/path comparison [lem-coef-kan-pullback-path-comparison] applies to $p_W^{\mathrm{eq}}$ as well. Maps of Segal spaces preserve these unions because $hf$ is a functor.

source.place: Lemma 5.8 and diagram (6.3): equivalence-arrow endpoint fibration

proof.text: Put $A=W_0$, $K_A=\operatorname{Fun}(\Delta^1,A)$ and $q_A=(\operatorname{ev}_0,\operatorname{ev}_1):K_A\to A^2$. Apply the Mathlib leaf [lem-cbc-internal-hom-fibration-corner-map] to the monomorphism $\partial\Delta^1\hookrightarrow\Delta^1$ and the Kan fibration $A\to\Delta^0$. Its target is $\operatorname{Fun}(\partial\Delta^1,A)=A^2$, so it gives exactly the endpoint fibration $q_A$. Filling a horn in $A^2$ coordinatewise and then lifting it along $q_A$ proves $K_A$ Kan. Apply [lem-coef-space-path-fibration-replacement] to $1_A$: its total space $A\times_{A,\operatorname{ev}_0}K_A$ is isomorphic to $K_A$ by projection, with inverse $\gamma\mapsto(\gamma(0),\gamma)$. Its weak equivalence is therefore precisely the constant-path map $c_A:A\to K_A$, and $q_Ac_A=\Delta_A$ by evaluation.

source.place: Proposition 6.4 (1) => (4) and Corollary 6.5, with an explicit natural path-model zigzag

proof.text: Completeness gives the weak equivalence $s_0:A\to W_{\mathrm{eq}}$ over $A^2$, and step 3 gives the weak equivalence $c_A$ over that same base. Apply [lem-coef-complete-segal-path-fiber-comparison]. Its specified zigzag compares $E_W(x,y)$ with $\operatorname{Path}_A(x,y)=\operatorname{fib}_{(x,y)}q_A$, naturally in maps of complete Segal spaces. For $x=y$ it preserves the identity-arrow and constant-loop basepoints. Thus later comparisons use the actual induced path map and its actual constant-loop basepoint.

source.place: Proposition 6.4 (1) => (4) and Corollary 6.5, with an explicit natural path-model zigzag

proof.text: Vertices of $\operatorname{Path}_A(x,y)$ are exactly edges $x\to y$. Such an edge exists precisely when $x,y$ are in the same simplicial component: reverse an edge by filling a two-dimensional outer horn with its edge and a degenerate edge, and compose two consecutive edges by filling $\Lambda_1^2$. This compresses any finite unoriented edge-chain to one edge. The component identification of [lem-coef-kan-realization-serre] identifies these classes with components of $|A|$. Along the zigzag of step 4 nonemptiness is preserved, because a simplicial set is nonempty exactly when it has a vertex, and a weak equivalence is bijective on components. Hence $E_W(x,y)$ is nonempty precisely when $x,y$ are in the same component of $A$.

source.place: Proposition 6.4 (1) => (4) and Corollary 6.5, with an explicit natural path-model zigzag

proof.text:
Suppose all $f_n$ are weak equivalences. Then $f_0\times f_0$ is a weak equivalence: [lem-coef-realization-finite-limits] identifies the realization of each simplicial product with the product in k-spaces, naturally in $f_0$. A path or a based cube into this product is exactly a pair of coordinate paths or based cubes; the same holds for their homotopies. These domains are compact Hausdorff, so passing from the topological product to its k-space topology changes none of these maps. Thus components and every based homotopy group are the products of the coordinate sets and groups, and the induced product maps are bijections and isomorphisms. Apply [lem-coef-spaces-homotopy-fiber-detection] to the endpoint square with top map $f_1$ and base map $f_0\times f_0$. Using the natural strict/path comparisons in [lem-coef-kan-pullback-path-comparison], its fiber map is the required weak equivalence $M_U(x,y)\to M_V(fx,fy)$.

To check essential surjectivity, surjectivity of $\pi_0f_0$ and the Kan component identification of [lem-coef-kan-realization-serre] give, for any vertex $b\in V_0$, a vertex $x\in U_0$ and an edge $\gamma:fx\to b$ in $V_0$ (replace an edge-chain by one edge with Kan horns). Lift the base edge $(\mathrm{const}_{fx},\gamma)$ through $p_V:V_1\to V_0^2$, specifying its initial point to be $s_0(fx)$. This is the lifting problem against $\Lambda_0^1=\{0\}\hookrightarrow\Delta^1$. Its terminal point is an arrow $g:fx\to b$, connected in $V_1$ to the identity of $fx$. By [lem-coef-segal-homotopy-category-components], $g$ represents an isomorphism. This proves essential surjectivity by an actual arrow with the required distinct endpoints.

source.place: Proposition 7.6 forward implication; Lemma 5.8 supplies invertibility after lifting the endpoint path

proof.text:
Conversely, assume the mapping-space condition and essential surjectivity. The component maps of the mapping-space weak equivalences are bijections, so the functor $hf:hU\to hV$ is fully faithful. It preserves and reflects isomorphisms: if $hf([a])$ has inverse $b$, fullness lifts $b$ to a class $c$ in the opposite hom-set, and faithfulness applied to $ca$ and $ac$ gives both inverse equations. Therefore the bijection $\pi_0M_U(x,y)\to\pi_0M_V(fx,fy)$ takes precisely the isomorphism components onto the isomorphism components. Its restriction
$$E_U(x,y)\longrightarrow E_V(fx,fy)$$
is a weak equivalence. To verify this last assertion directly, it is bijective on the selected components, and on every positive homotopy group it has the same isomorphism as the original map: a based sphere, cube or homotopy is connected and consequently stays inside the component containing its basepoint. The identification of these $E$ spaces as strict equivalence-arrow fibers uses [lem-coef-segal-homotopy-category-components]. No assertion about fibers at pairs outside the image of $f_0$ is needed.

source.place: Proposition 7.6: full faithfulness reflects isomorphisms and restricts mapping-space equivalences

proof.text: By the zigzag of step 4, two vertices of $W_0$ belong to the same component if and only if $E_W(x,y)$ is nonempty, equivalently if and only if they are isomorphic in $hW$. Essential surjectivity thus makes $\pi_0f_0$ surjective. For injectivity, if $fx$ and $fy$ are in the same component of $V_0$, they are isomorphic in $hV$. Full faithfulness from step 7 lifts this isomorphism and its inverse and reflects their inverse equations, so $x,y$ are isomorphic in $hU$ and hence lie in the same component of $U_0$. This proves that $\pi_0f_0$ is bijective, including the empty case.

source.place: Corollary 6.5 and the first sentence of the converse proof of Proposition 7.6

proof.text:
Write $A=U_0$, $B=V_0$, and $g=f_0$. The mapping-space hypothesis and step 7 give, for every vertex $x$ of $A$, a weak equivalence
$$E_U(x,x)\longrightarrow E_V(gx,gx).$$
The natural zigzag of step 4 commutes with $f$, including its identity and constant-loop basepoints. Two-out-of-three therefore gives a weak equivalence
$$\operatorname{Path}_A(x,x)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Path}_B(gx,gx),$$
which is the pointed loop map $\Omega_xA\to\Omega_{gx}B$. This argument uses only the strict/path comparisons and completeness zigzag; it does not assume that $g$ is already a weak equivalence and does not invoke a total-space fiber criterion. The path-fibration replacement of step 3 identifies these strict fibers with the corresponding homotopy fibers, so the comparison is natural in the chosen vertex and in maps of complete Segal spaces.

source.place: Proposition 7.6 right square and large rectangle; explicit common-base fibration replacement of the diagonal square

proof.text:
The loop equivalences of step 9 and the component bijection of step 8 imply that $g:A\to B$ is a weak homotopy equivalence as follows. For each vertex $x\in A$ and every $j\geq0$, use the natural boundary bijections of [lem-coef-kan-path-boundary-bijections]
$$\pi_{j+1}^s(A,x)\cong\pi_j^s(\Omega_xA,c_x),\qquad \pi_{j+1}^s(B,gx)\cong\pi_j^s(\Omega_{gx}B,c_{gx}).$$
The map between their right sides is a bijection, for $j=0$ by the component comparison of [lem-coef-kan-realization-serre], and for $j\geq1$ by its simplicial/realized homotopy-group comparison and the loop weak equivalence. Naturality of the boundary maps gives bijectivity of the map on $\pi_{j+1}^s$ on the left; these maps are group homomorphisms, so they are isomorphisms. The same realization comparison gives isomorphisms on all positive homotopy groups of $|A|\to|B|$ at vertices. Any point in a realization has a representative in a simplex and is connected inside that simplex to a vertex. For a path $\gamma$ from a source vertex $x$ to a source point $a$, [lem-coef-homotopy-groups-basepoint-change] gives isomorphisms $\beta_\gamma$ and $\beta_{|g|\gamma}$. Their displayed concentric-cube formula commutes with postcomposition: applying $|g|$ to its inner cube gives the inner cube for $|g|\circ u$, and applying $|g|$ to its outer shell gives the shell along $|g|\gamma$. Consequently $\beta_{|g|\gamma}\circ |g|_{*,a}=|g|_{*,x}\circ\beta_\gamma$, so the isomorphism at $x$ implies the isomorphism at $a$. Together with the already proved component bijection this is precisely the definition of weak homotopy equivalence. Thus $f_0=g$ is a weak equivalence; this supplies the degree-zero conclusion, rather than citing a pasting argument as its proof.

source.place: Expanded final inference of Proposition 7.6: natural loop-boundary bijections and the definition of weak homotopy equivalence

proof.text: Now $f_0\times f_0$ is a weak equivalence by the coordinatewise product argument of step 6. Apply [lem-coef-spaces-homotopy-fiber-detection] to the endpoint square, using the assumed mapping-space equivalences and [lem-coef-kan-pullback-path-comparison], to conclude that $f_1$ is a weak equivalence. For $n\geq2$, form the consecutive-edge fiber products one factor at a time. The endpoint maps $W_1\to W_0$ are Kan fibrations because $p_W$ is one and projection from $W_0^2$ is one; composites and pullbacks of horn-lifting maps are horn-lifting maps, by successively solving the same lifting problems. Thus each intermediate edge product is Kan, and each strict pullback in the construction compares naturally with its path-model homotopy pullback by [lem-coef-kan-pullback-path-comparison]. Inductively [lem-coef-kan-homotopy-pullback-invariance], with the established equivalences $f_0$ and $f_1$, makes the map of $n$-edge products a weak equivalence. The commuting Segal comparison maps from $U_n,V_n$ are weak equivalences by hypothesis; two-out-of-three now gives that $f_n$ is a weak equivalence. This proves every degree and completes both implications.

old_proof.text:
Here is the natural consequence of completeness needed later, with its fiber comparison made explicit. Put $A=W_0$, $K_A=\operatorname{Fun}(\Delta^1,A)$, $q_A=(\operatorname{ev}_0,\operatorname{ev}_1):K_A\to A^2$, and let $c_A:A\to K_A$ insert constant paths. The endpoint map $q_A$ is a Kan fibration: a horn-lifting problem for it is adjoint to extending a map from $(\Lambda_i^m\times\Delta^1)\cup(\Delta^m\times\partial\Delta^1)$ to $\Delta^m\times\Delta^1$; this inclusion is anodyne by [lem-coef-sset-anodyne-pushout-product], since the horn inclusion is anodyne in [lem-coef-kan-quillen-right-proper]. Its target $A$ is Kan, so the extension exists. In particular $K_A$ is Kan. For the identity map of $A$, the replacement in [lem-coef-space-path-fibration-replacement] identifies with $K_A$, and its constant-path inclusion is exactly $c_A$, hence is a weak equivalence.

The maps $s_0:A\to W_{\mathrm{eq}}$ and $c_A:A\to K_A$ lie over $A^2$, with source structure map $\Delta_A$. Both are weak equivalences, the first by completeness. Apply [lem-coef-spaces-homotopy-fiber-detection] twice with base map $1_{A^2}$, and then [lem-coef-kan-pullback-path-comparison] for the two endpoint fibrations. For every pair $(x,y)$ this gives a natural zigzag of weak equivalences
$$E_W(x,y)\longrightarrow\operatorname{hofib}_{(x,y)}(p_W^{\mathrm{eq}})\longleftarrow\operatorname{hofib}_{(x,y)}(\Delta_A)\longrightarrow\operatorname{hofib}_{(x,y)}(q_A)\longleftarrow\operatorname{Path}_A(x,y),$$
where $\operatorname{Path}_A(x,y)$ is the strict fiber of $q_A$. The arrows use constant paths, $s_0$, and $c_A$, so this zigzag commutes with every map of complete Segal spaces, including the basepoint given by the identity and the constant loop when $x=y$. It follows that $E_W(x,y)$ is nonempty exactly when $x$ and $y$ belong to the same component of $A$. Indeed a nonempty Kan complex has a vertex, weak equivalences preserve nonemptiness through their bijections on components, and vertices of the path space are edges $x\to y$; an edge-chain in a Kan complex is replaced by one edge using successive two-dimensional horn fillers.

Then $f_0\times f_0$ is a weak equivalence: [lem-coef-realization-finite-limits] identifies the realization of each simplicial product with the product in k-spaces, naturally in $f_0$. A path or a based cube into this product is exactly a pair of coordinate paths or based cubes; the same holds for their homotopies. These domains are compact Hausdorff, so passing from the topological product to its k-space topology changes none of these maps. Thus components and every based homotopy group are the products of the coordinate sets and groups, and the induced product maps are bijections and isomorphisms. Apply [lem-coef-spaces-homotopy-fiber-detection] to the endpoint square with top map $f_1$ and base map $f_0\times f_0$. Using the natural strict/path comparisons in [lem-coef-kan-pullback-path-comparison], its fiber map is the required weak equivalence $M_U(x,y)\to M_V(fx,fy)$.

To check essential surjectivity, surjectivity of $\pi_0f_0$ and the Kan component identification of [lem-coef-kan-realization-serre] give, for any vertex $b\in V_0$, a vertex $x\in U_0$ and an edge $\gamma:fx\to b$ in $V_0$ (replace an edge-chain by one edge with Kan horns). Lift the base edge $(\mathrm{const}_{fx},\gamma)$ through $p_V:V_1\to V_0^2$, specifying its initial point to be $s_0(fx)$. This is the lifting problem against $\Lambda_0^1=\{0\}\hookrightarrow\Delta^1$. Its terminal point is an arrow $g:fx\to b$, connected in $V_1$ to the identity of $fx$. By [lem-coef-segal-homotopy-category-components], $g$ represents an isomorphism. This proves essential surjectivity by an actual arrow with the required distinct endpoints.

old_proof.text:
Conversely, assume the mapping-space condition and essential surjectivity. The component maps of the mapping-space weak equivalences are bijections, so the functor $hf:hU\to hV$ is fully faithful. It preserves and reflects isomorphisms: if $hf([a])$ has inverse $b$, fullness lifts $b$ to a class $c$ in the opposite hom-set, and faithfulness applied to $ca$ and $ac$ gives both inverse equations. Therefore the bijection $\pi_0M_U(x,y)\to\pi_0M_V(fx,fy)$ takes precisely the isomorphism components onto the isomorphism components. Its restriction
$$E_U(x,y)\longrightarrow E_V(fx,fy)$$
is a weak equivalence. To verify this last assertion directly, it is bijective on the selected components, and on every positive homotopy group it has the same isomorphism as the original map: a based sphere, cube or homotopy is connected and consequently stays inside the component containing its basepoint. The identification of these $E$ spaces as strict equivalence-arrow fibers uses [lem-coef-segal-homotopy-category-components]. No assertion about fibers at pairs outside the image of $f_0$ is needed.

old_proof.text: By the zigzag of step 3, two vertices of $W_0$ belong to the same component if and only if $E_W(x,y)$ is nonempty, equivalently if and only if they are isomorphic in $hW$. Essential surjectivity thus makes $\pi_0f_0$ surjective. For injectivity, if $fx$ and $fy$ are in the same component of $V_0$, they are isomorphic in $hV$. Full faithfulness from step 5 lifts this isomorphism and its inverse and reflects their inverse equations, so $x,y$ are isomorphic in $hU$ and hence lie in the same component of $U_0$. This proves that $\pi_0f_0$ is bijective, including the empty case.

old_proof.text:
Write $A=U_0$, $B=V_0$, and $g=f_0$. First the usual endpoint square is a homotopy pullback. The comparison $U_1\to A^2\times_{B^2}V_1$ is a map of Kan fibrations over $A^2$, and its fiber at $(x,y)$ is the given map $M_U(x,y)\to M_V(gx,gy)$. It is a weak equivalence by [lem-coef-kan-fibration-arbitrary-base-fibers]; the strict pullback computes the homotopy pullback by [lem-coef-kan-pullback-path-comparison]. For equivalence arrows, form $U_{\mathrm{eq}}\to A^2\times_{B^2}V_{\mathrm{eq}}$ over $A^2$. Both structure maps are Kan fibrations by step 2 and pullback stability of horn lifting; the fiber map at $(x,y)$ is $E_U(x,y)\to E_V(gx,gy)$, a weak equivalence by step 5. Applying [lem-coef-kan-fibration-arbitrary-base-fibers] makes this total comparison a weak equivalence, and [lem-coef-kan-pullback-path-comparison] identifies its strict target with the homotopy pullback.

Here are the details for replacing that top row by $A,B$ via completeness, without assuming that $g$ is already a weak equivalence. In the natural zigzag of step 3 the $E$ map is a weak equivalence by step 5. Two-out-of-three in the commuting zigzag implies that
$$\operatorname{hofib}_{(x,y)}(\Delta_A)\longrightarrow\operatorname{hofib}_{(gx,gy)}(\Delta_B)$$
is a weak equivalence for every $(x,y)\in A^2$. Use [lem-coef-space-path-fibration-replacement] to factor each diagonal as $A\xrightarrow{\sim}D_A\twoheadrightarrow A^2$ and $B\xrightarrow{\sim}D_B\twoheadrightarrow B^2$. The comparison $D_A\to A^2\times_{B^2}D_B$ is a map of fibrations over the common base $A^2$ with exactly these homotopy-fiber maps. It is a weak equivalence by [lem-coef-kan-fibration-arbitrary-base-fibers]. Composing with $A\to D_A$ proves explicitly that the diagonal square, whose rows are $\Delta_A:A\to A^2$ and $\Delta_B:B\to B^2$ and whose columns are $g$ and $g\times g$, is a homotopy pullback. Further, the other end of the same natural zigzag gives weak equivalences $\operatorname{Path}_A(x,y)\to\operatorname{Path}_B(gx,gy)$. For $y=x$ this is exactly the pointed loop map $\Omega_x A\to\Omega_{gx}B$, based at the constant loop.

old_proof.text:
The loop equivalences of step 7 and the component bijection of step 6 imply that $g:A\to B$ is a weak homotopy equivalence as follows. For each vertex $x\in A$ and every $j\geq0$, use the natural boundary bijections of [lem-coef-kan-path-boundary-bijections]
$$\pi_{j+1}^s(A,x)\cong\pi_j^s(\Omega_xA,c_x),\qquad \pi_{j+1}^s(B,gx)\cong\pi_j^s(\Omega_{gx}B,c_{gx}).$$
The map between their right sides is a bijection, for $j=0$ by the component comparison of [lem-coef-kan-realization-serre], and for $j\geq1$ by its simplicial/realized homotopy-group comparison and the loop weak equivalence. Naturality of the boundary maps gives bijectivity of the map on $\pi_{j+1}^s$ on the left; these maps are group homomorphisms, so they are isomorphisms. The same realization comparison gives isomorphisms on all positive homotopy groups of $|A|\to|B|$ at vertices. Any point in a realization has a representative in a simplex and is connected inside that simplex to a vertex. For a path $\gamma$ from a source vertex $x$ to a source point $a$, [lem-coef-homotopy-groups-basepoint-change] gives isomorphisms $\beta_\gamma$ and $\beta_{|g|\gamma}$. Their displayed concentric-cube formula commutes with postcomposition: applying $|g|$ to its inner cube gives the inner cube for $|g|\circ u$, and applying $|g|$ to its outer shell gives the shell along $|g|\gamma$. Consequently $\beta_{|g|\gamma}\circ |g|_{*,a}=|g|_{*,x}\circ\beta_\gamma$, so the isomorphism at $x$ implies the isomorphism at $a$. Together with the already proved component bijection this is precisely the definition of weak homotopy equivalence. Thus $f_0=g$ is a weak equivalence; this supplies the degree-zero conclusion, rather than citing a pasting argument as its proof.

old_proof.text: Now $f_0\times f_0$ is a weak equivalence by the coordinatewise product argument of step 4. Apply [lem-coef-spaces-homotopy-fiber-detection] to the endpoint square, using the assumed mapping-space equivalences and [lem-coef-kan-pullback-path-comparison], to conclude that $f_1$ is a weak equivalence. For $n\geq2$, form the consecutive-edge fiber products one factor at a time. The endpoint maps $W_1\to W_0$ are Kan fibrations because $p_W$ is one and projection from $W_0^2$ is one; composites and pullbacks of horn-lifting maps are horn-lifting maps, by successively solving the same lifting problems. Thus each intermediate edge product is Kan, and each strict pullback in the construction compares naturally with its path-model homotopy pullback by [lem-coef-kan-pullback-path-comparison]. Inductively [lem-coef-kan-homotopy-pullback-invariance], with the established equivalences $f_0$ and $f_1$, makes the map of $n$-edge products a weak equivalence. The commuting Segal comparison maps from $U_n,V_n$ are weak equivalences by hypothesis; two-out-of-three now gives that $f_n$ is a weak equivalence. This proves every degree and completes both implications.
